title: Faith seeking understanding
hookLine: Anselm of Canterbury: I believe so that I may understand

lines: A MONK WHO CAN'T PUT A QUESTION DOWN.
HE WRITES IT AS A PRAYER.
cards: A monk in Normandy can't put a question down. He's Anselm, prior of the abbey of Bec, and one day he'll be archbishop of Canterbury. He had already written one book about God at his brothers' request.
Now he wanted something that sounds simple: a single short argument. By his own account he searched, nearly gave up, and tried to push the idea away like a distraction. It wouldn't leave.
His biographer says it troubled his sleep, his meals, even his prayers. Then, one night, it came clear. He wrote it down, not as a lecture, but as a prayer, spoken to God.

teach.b: Anselm called the book the Proslogion, an address. In its preface he says his first title for it was faith seeking understanding. Its first chapter ends with words people still quote.

teach.h: I BELIEVE SO THAT I MAY UNDERSTAND.
teach.b: In paraphrase: I don't try to understand so that I can believe. I believe so that I can understand. In Latin, credo ut intelligam.
Hear what that does and doesn't say. It doesn't say: switch off your mind and believe. And it doesn't say: believe nothing until it's proven.
Faith comes first, and then faith goes looking. It asks. It argues.
It wants to know what it loves. Watch how the book begins. Before any argument, Anselm invites himself to step away from his busy thoughts for a little while and seek God's face.
Then he reasons, out loud, in front of God. The New Testament has its own version.

The first letter of Peter, in the King James words, asks believers to "be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you." A reason for the hope, not a slogan.
Then a monk named Gaunilo read Anselm's argument and wrote a reply, pushing back hard.

teach.h: THE CRITIC'S REPLY GOES IN THE BOOK.
teach.b: Anselm answered him, and asked that the critic's reply and his own response travel together with the book. Questions welcomed, answers shown in public. Christians use the motto in different ways.
Some theologians build whole systems on it. For other readers it's simpler: belief and questions can sit at the same table.

how: Christians often bring questions about faith to study groups, classes, books and conversations with pastors or priests, and Anselm's phrase is still used to describe theology as faith that asks questions.

games.q: you're Anselm. a monk named Gaunilo has written a reply attacking your argument. what do you do?
o: ignore it and hope it fades.
answer it, and have both replies copied with your book.
ask your monks not to read it.
games.why: Anselm answered Gaunilo and asked that the critic's reply and his own response be added to the book. questions welcomed, answers shown in public.

practice: Let a question rise that you don't usually say out loud, about God, about something you were taught, about why you're on this path at all, and ask it plainly in your own words, without answering it yet.
If you pray, ask it in prayer, the way Anselm spoke his straight to God; if you don't, hold it like an object in your hands and turn it over slowly. Questions are welcome here.
